name: Benyadu' / Banyaduq, Sangke village variety
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Jardine, Adam, Angeliki Athanasopoulou, Kristian & Peter Cole. 2015. Banyaduq prestopped nasals: Synchrony and diachrony. Oceanic Linguistics 54(2): 548-578. doi:10.1353/ol.2015.0018. Quoted from the author's accepted manuscript (Aug 2015, 36 pp.),http://adamjardine.net/files/jardineetalbanyaduq-aug15manuscript.pdf
catalog_locator: Author's accepted manuscript of 36 (ms p.16), sec. 4.1.5 'Alternative analyses' (section heading on ms p.15), the second full paragraph on p.16, beginning 'One last possible predictor for the distribution of prestopped nasals might be suprasegmental', immediately before the cophonology paragraph and heading 4.1.6 on the same page; file rendered (page render) and read by both checks; published Oceanic Linguistics pagination (548-578) not verified
catalog_quote: One last possible predictor for the distribution of prestopped nasals might be suprasegmental. This is not plausible, however, as Banyaduq has neither contrastive stress nor tone. It is beyond the purview of this paper to discuss whether Banyaduq has stress at all, but descriptively, final vowels are consistently pronounced with slightly higher duration and intensity. For example, the final [u] is prominent in both (25b) [ŋãrum] ‘night’ and (23c) [mõrupm] ‘to fly.’ Stress cannot, then, provide an explanation for why only the latter has a prestopped nasal. Thus, consistent triggers do not exist, either segmentally or suprasegmentally, which could justify positing an NPG-like explanation for the distribution of plain and prestopped nasals.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive and there is no tone; the authors do not commit to whether word stress exists, but the final vowel of the word is consistently the most prominent (greater duration and intensity), i.e. descriptively final prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None; final prominence is called consistent. Caveat: the authors explicitly leave open whether this prominence should be analysed as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms and elicited/recorded words of the Sangke dialect); the paper is about prestopped nasals, and stress is treated only in passing. One transcription in the quote ([ŋaru]) is reconstructed from the extracted text output where a character was dropped.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Sangke Banyaduq (village of Sangke, southern Landak Regency), the native variety of co-author Kristian; the paper also uses Panchi' (Hudson 1970) and Temahar (Suhardi 2005) wordlists and notes phonological differences among these dialects. Glottolog beny1237 has no dialect subdivisions. 'Banyaduq' = Glottolog 'Benyadu'' = Indonesian 'Dayak Banyadu''; Smith 2017 places it in a Benyadu-Bekati subgroup of Land Dayak.
